spans.content: Prediction of lower limb kinematics from vision-based system using
deep learning approaches
Konki Sravan Kumar<sup>1</sup>, Ankhzaya Jamsrandorj<sup>2</sup>, Jinwook Kim<sup>1</sup> and Kyung-Ryoul Mun<sup>1</sup>
Abstract— The joint angular velocity during daily life
exercises is an important clinical outcome for injury risk
index, rehabilitation progress monitoring and athlete’s
performance evaluation. Recently, wearable sensors have been
widely used to monitor lower limb kinematics. However, these
sensors are difficult and inconvenient to use in daily life. To
mitigate these limitations, this study proposes a vision-based
system for estimating lower limb joint kinematics using a deep
convolution neural network with bi-directional long-short term
memory and gated recurrent unit network. The normalized
correlation coefficient, and the mean absolute error were
computed between the ground truth obtained from the optical
motion capture system and estimated joint angular velocities
using proposed models. The estimated results show a highest
correlation 0.93 in squat and 0.92 in walking on treadmill
action. Furthermore, independent model for each joint angular
velocity at the hip, knee, and ankle were analyzed and
compared. Among the three joint angular velocities, knee
joint has a best estimated accuracy (0.96 in squat and 0.96 in
walking on the treadmill). The proposed models show higher
estimation accuracy under both the lateral and the frontal
view regardless of the camera positions and angles. This
study proves the applicability of using sensor free vision-based
system to monitor the lower limb kinematics during home
workouts for healthcare and rehabilitation.
I. INTRODUCTION
Human gait is pattern of movement of the limbs, and
gait parameters can reflect the human’s functional ability
and health condition [1]. Among the several gait parameters,
the lower body joint angular velocity during daily life
exercises is an important clinical outcome for injury risk
index, determine the progress during the rehabilitation of
patients, diagnose early human joint movement disorders
and improve athlete’s performance [2, 3]. In addition, recent
studies have identified that [4, 5] joint angular velocity is the
strong candidate for monitoring changes in lower limb joint
powers because the joint power is a product of joint angular
velocity and joint motion, which is significant parameter for
clinical diagnosis of gait pathology and control of lower limb
prosthesis [6, 7]. Inertial sensor-based systems are commonly
used to capture the lower limb kinematics. An inertial mea-
surement unit (IMU) sensor based system is designed to mea-
sure the knee joint angles during the human limb dynamic
movement [8]. An IMU sensor-based 3D motion capture
system composed of an accelerator, geomagnetic sensor and
gyroscopes are effective measurement tools to record lower
limb joints (knee, hip, and spine) motion during daily life ac-
tions [9]. Over the last few years, IMU sensor-based systems
have drawn researcher’s attention and showed significant
accuracy in joint kinematic measurements [10, 11]. However,
one IMU sensor cannot be used to track movements of more
than one body segment. Therefore, seven IMU sensors are
usually required to track just for a lower limb movement
such as pelvis, ankle, knee, and hip of each left and right
side. As more IMU sensors are attached, several drawback
include complex preprocessing processes (sensor-to-segment
calibration and subject calibration), inconvenience to daily
life and human kinematic chains that should be considered
to monitor accurate lower limb kinematics [12]. In addition,
the use of motion tracking systems like IMU sensors hinde
the natural movements of the subjects due to tight straps
for the sensor attachment, and it is still expensive, power
consumption, complex handling of equipment, participant
cooperation and controlled laboratory environment and plac
ing markers, which are labor-intensive. Researchers have
developed camera-based system to overcome the limitation
of wearable sensor-based capture systems to monitor human
low limb motion. The emerged deep learning framework
and development of camera technology had created a new
opportunity for lower limb angular velocity prediction from
video frame information. Recent studies [13, 14] were intro
duced a camera-based system using the OpenPose library,
which records lower limb joint angles with good accuracy.
However, the estimation accuracy of OpenPose library-based
system relies on ground truth 2D keypoint dataset; keypoints
are manually annotated and not at joint center positions.
Therefore, it may not be reliable to estimate lower limb
angular velocity. Moreover, these methods were developed
to monitor joint angles of the participants only in lateral
view and cannot track joint angles in front and back view
of subjects. In our previous study, deep convolution neural
network CNN architecture has been proposed to measure
the lower angular velocity of the hip, knee, and ankle
joints, which offers good estimation accuracy under differen
camera views [15]. However, these pre-trained deep CNN
frameworks still show higher errors due to time delay in the
estimation results
In this study, we propose a vision-based system for estima-
tion of lower limb joint kinematics with a deep convolution
neural network with bi-directional long-short term mem-

(DeepConvLSTM/ DeepConvGRU). The proposed approach
is based on an RGB camera system, which detects the joint

II. METHODS
A. Experimental Equipment and Protocol
To build the video dataset, participants were recruited by
33 healthy adult (25 – male and 8 – female). Experiments
were conducted in an experimental room installed with the
optical motion capture system and Xiaomi Mijia Camera
4K digital camera system. Fig.1. shows the arrangement of
cameras during our experiments to obtain a video dataset.
As the gold standard for recording human joint angles, a six
camera optical motion capture system with a resolution of
1280×1024 (around 1.3 million pixels) and a frequency of
120Hz was used. According to the Plug-in-gait marker set,
fifteen reflective markers were attached to the human limbs
such as pelvis, hip, knee, thigh, shank, toe, ankle, and heel.
The optical motion capture system tracks reflective markers
attached to the human body and carries out the accurate
3D angles and 3D positions of all joints. The joint angular
velocities are calculated by derivation of the joint angles. The
capture area is 2.000 meters by 3.685 meters on the floor.
Six cameras of digital camera system with a resolution of
1920×1080 and, a frame rate of 60Hz was used. Six cameras
were placed in front, back and side of a participant to capture
videos of squat and walking on treadmill actions within 30
seconds. We designed a digital circuit to synchronize the
optical motion capture camera and digital camera systems.
The optical motion capture camera system has samples
of 120 frames per second (twice the value of the digital
camera’s frame rate. Therefore, Annotations were down-
sampled with the frame rate of 120Hz to 60Hz.
Fig. 1: Experimental setup. The optical motion captures system
tracks the markers, records the angular velocity of joints and digital
cameras captures video information of participants during squat and
walking on treadmill actions.
B. Deep learning framework for estimating the Joint angular
velocity of lower limbs.
We propose a deep learning model (DeepConvLSTM)
based on the CNN with LSTM neural network to estimate
angular velocities of lower limb joints such as hips, knees,
and ankles on both the right and left sides. The convolutional
neural network is used to extract features (spatial domain)
from the action video, while recurrent neural network is used
to provide time-series prediction (time-domain). As a super-
vised manner, DeepConvLSTM architecture learns the time
dependencies between RGB image information as inputs and
joint angular velocities as outputs. First, deep learning-based
feature selection technique (YOLO4) is applied to detect the
human and remove the non-informative background in the
action videos [16]. Then, the video frames were cropped
based on the resultant human bounding box and resized to
448 × 448. Next, a 27 video frame information is considered
input of the proposed DeepConvLSTM network. Then, the
network is trained to output the corresponding six joint
angular velocities. In this work, we employed a convolutional
neural network (ResNet18) with the Bi-LSTM / GRU to
predict the joint angular velocity estimation. At each time
step, the extracted spatial feature from CNN layer is con-
nected to LSTM/GRU network. Finally, the fully connected
(FC) layer provides the six joint angular velocity predictions
(left/ right hip flexion/extension, knee flexion/extension, and
ankle dorsiflexion/plantarflexion) at each time step as shown
in Fig.2.
Fig. 2: The DeepConvLSTM architecture. Deep CNN extracts
features (spatial domain) from the action video and LSTM is
used to provide time-series (time-domain) joint angular velocity
predictions.

The DeepConvLSTM was implemented using the PyTorch

using Ubuntu 18.04.5 LTS. The learning rate for the training
network was selected to be 0.0001. The batch size was 8, and

III. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
This section presents results of proposed DeepConvLSTM/
DeepConvGRU network for predicting lower limb joint
angular velocities during squat and walking on treadmill ac-
tions. The difference between the angular velocities obtained
from the optical motion capture system and the estimated
by the DeepConvLSTM and DeepConvGRU networks were
evaluated with the normalized correlation coefficients (r),
and the mean absolute error (MAE). To illustrate the esti-
mation performance of the proposed models, Fig.3. shows
estimated and ground-truth angular velocities at lower limb
joints during squat action. The estimated angular velocities
using DeepConvGRU were better than those estimated by
ResNet18 and DeepConvLSTM compared to ground truth
angular velocities. The predicted angular velocities during
walking on a treadmill are depicted in Fig. 4. The average
of r for all the three joints of GRU, BI-LSTM and ResNet18
networks during squat and walking on a treadmill are re-
ported in detail in Table I. The average of r of the GRU
network shows a strong correlation (0.93 during squat and
0.92 during walking on treadmill) among all three models.
The average r and MAE for the joint-wise angular velocity
at the hip, knee, and ankle during squat were predicted by
three models are presented in Table II. Among the hip, knee
and ankle joints, the knee joint angular velocity estimated
using the GRU model showed better accuracy in the average
r. The GRU network offers a less MAE error than BI-LSTM
and ResNet18 networks in all joint estimations during squat
action.

IV. DISCUSSION
This study introduced a vision-based system using Deep-
ConvLSTM/ DeepConvGRU network for estimating the
lower limb joint angular velocities during squat and walking
on treadmill actions. We conducted the experimental study
with the optical motion capture system to record the angular
velocity and Xiaomi Mijia Camera 4K digital camera system
to capture the video of actions. The proposed architectures
were trained with action video information as inputs and
corresponding joint angular velocities as outputs. To train the
proposed models, Action videos of seven participants during
a squat and walking on a treadmill were used for training,
action videos of three participants for validation and three
participants for testing. The difference between the angular
velocities obtained from the optical motion capture system
and the estimated by the DeepConvLSTM and DeepCon-
vGRU networks were evaluated with r, and the MAE. The r
measures correlation between the and estimated and ground
truth angular velocities. The predicted joint angular velocities
using DeepConvLSTM/ DeepConvGRU network showed a
quite good match with the angular velocities obtained using
an optical motion capture system during squat and walking
on treadmill actions.
A reported in Table I, DeepConvGRU model provided the
highest accuracy among the three deep learning architectures,
0.93 in squat and 0.92 in walking on treadmill action. The
estimation performance of the independent DeepConvLSTM/
DeepConvGRU models were evaluated for each hip, knee,
and ankle joint angular velocity during squat and walking
on a treadmill actions. The DeepConvGRU network offers
a higher r in both actions. Among the three joint angular
velocities, the estimated knee joint shows higher accuracy
(0.96 in squat and 0.96 in walking on the treadmill) than the
estimated hip and ankle joint angular velocities. The knee
joint motion in the sagittal plane is more stable between
participants and the ankle joint having a higher degree of
freedom; the hip joint estimation accuracy may affect by
variations in physical measurements of the participants and
motion artifacts due to the fluctuations of the marker at
the hip joint. The average r for angular velocities of three
participants under lateral and frontal camera views is demon-
strated in Table IV. The average r in both lateral and front
views is more than 0.90, showing that the DeepConvGRU
network offers relatively higher prediction accuracy in both
camera views regardless of the camera positions and angles.
The average MAE for the hip, knee and ankle joint angular
velocity during squat and walking on a treadmill action. The
average of MAE of GRU network offers a less error than
BI-LSTM and ResNet18 networks during squat and walking
on treadmill as reported in Table II and Table III. However,
proposed models still show higher MAE error due to lack
of accuracy in ground truth angular velocities captured by
motion captured system and an offset value error can be
generated from the imprecise positions of makers on the
human body, and variations in physical measurements of
the participants. The proposed DeepConvGRU model shows
angular velocity error between 15 to 20 rad/s. Although, the
higher MAE error limitation was overcome to some degree
by applying a sequential network.
In our future work, the experiments should be conducted
with larger group of participants, different age groups, more
daily actions in different speeds and patients who have
undergone gait pathologies. The proposed DeepConvGRU
model will be extended to use of transformers and multi-head
attention based networks for much higher angular velocity
estimation. It is essential to confirm using other accurate
motion captured system for ground truth annotations. Our
work will be extended to estimate other gait parameter
(cadence, speed, stride length, and step width).
V. CONCLUSIONS
This paper presented a vision-based system for estimating
lower limb joint angular velocity during a squat and walking
on a treadmill action using Bi-LSTM and GRU recurrent
neural networks. The proposed architectures were trained
with action video information as inputs and corresponding
joint angular velocities as outputs. The joint angular veloc-
ities estimated using the DeepConvGRU network strongly
correlate with joint angular velocities measured using mo-
tion captured system and provides higher accuracy under
different camera views. These estimation results demonstrate
the potential to monitor joint angular velocities using video
information without wearable sensors. However, proposed
models still show angular velocity error between 15 to 20
rad/s due to lack of accuracy in ground truth angular veloc-
ities captured by motion-captured system. For much higher
angular velocity estimation, our work will be extended to use
of transformers and multi-head attention based networks. The
proposed vision- based method also would be applicable to
estimate other gait parameter (cadence, speed, stride length,
and step width).

IV. DISCUSSION
This study introduced a vision-based system using Deep-
ConvLSTM/ DeepConvGRU network for estimating the
lower limb joint angular velocities during squat and walking
on treadmill actions. We conducted the experimental study
with the optical motion capture system to record the angular
velocity and Xiaomi Mijia Camera 4K digital camera system
to capture the video of actions. The proposed architectures
were trained with action video information as inputs and
corresponding joint angular velocities as outputs. To train the
proposed models, Action videos of seven participants during
a squat and walking on a treadmill were used for training,
action videos of three participants for validation and three
participants for testing. The difference between the angular
velocities obtained from the optical motion capture system
and the estimated by the DeepConvLSTM and DeepCon-
vGRU networks were evaluated with r, and the MAE. The r
measures correlation between the and estimated and ground
truth angular velocities. The predicted joint angular velocities
using DeepConvLSTM/ DeepConvGRU network showed a
quite good match with the angular velocities obtained using
an optical motion capture system during squat and walking
on treadmill actions.
A reported in Table I, DeepConvGRU model provided the
highest accuracy among the three deep learning architectures,
0.93 in squat and 0.92 in walking on treadmill action. The
estimation performance of the independent DeepConvLSTM/
DeepConvGRU models were evaluated for each hip, knee,
and ankle joint angular velocity during squat and walking
on a treadmill actions. The DeepConvGRU network offers
a higher r in both actions. Among the three joint angular
velocities, the estimated knee joint shows higher accuracy
(0.96 in squat and 0.96 in walking on the treadmill) than the
estimated hip and ankle joint angular velocities. The knee
joint motion in the sagittal plane is more stable between
participants and the ankle joint having a higher degree of
freedom; the hip joint estimation accuracy may affect by
variations in physical measurements of the participants and
motion artifacts due to the fluctuations of the marker at
the hip joint. The average r for angular velocities of three
participants under lateral and frontal camera views is demon-
strated in Table IV. The average r in both lateral and front
views is more than 0.90, showing that the DeepConvGRU
network offers relatively higher prediction accuracy in both
camera views regardless of the camera positions and angles.
The average MAE for the hip, knee and ankle joint angular
velocity during squat and walking on a treadmill action. The
average of MAE of GRU network offers a less error than
BI-LSTM and ResNet18 networks during squat and walking
on treadmill as reported in Table II and Table III. However,
proposed models still show higher MAE error due to lack
of accuracy in ground truth angular velocities captured by
motion captured system and an offset value error can be
generated from the imprecise positions of makers on the
human body, and variations in physical measurements of
the participants. The proposed DeepConvGRU model shows
angular velocity error between 15 to 20 rad/s. Although, the
higher MAE error limitation was overcome to some degree
by applying a sequential network.
In our future work, the experiments should be conducted
with larger group of participants, different age groups, more
daily actions in different speeds and patients who have
undergone gait pathologies. The proposed DeepConvGRU
model will be extended to use of transformers and multi-head
attention based networks for much higher angular velocity
estimation. It is essential to confirm using other accurate
motion captured system for ground truth annotations. Our
work will be extended to estimate other gait parameter
(cadence, speed, stride length, and step width).
V. CONCLUSIONS
This paper presented a vision-based system for estimating
lower limb joint angular velocity during a squat and walking
on a treadmill action using Bi-LSTM and GRU recurrent
neural networks. The proposed architectures were trained
with action video information as inputs and corresponding
joint angular velocities as outputs. The joint angular veloc-
ities estimated using the DeepConvGRU network strongly
correlate with joint angular velocities measured using mo-
tion captured system and provides higher accuracy under
different camera views. These estimation results demonstrate
the potential to monitor joint angular velocities using video
information without wearable sensors. However, proposed
models still show angular velocity error between 15 to 20
rad/s due to lack of accuracy in ground truth angular veloc-
ities captured by motion-captured system. For much higher
angular velocity estimation, our work will be extended to use
of transformers and multi-head attention based networks. The
proposed vision- based method also would be applicable to
estimate other gait parameter (cadence, speed, stride length,
and step width).
